label: Cell Complexes
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 127 through 158 and builds spaces by gluing cells. We treat a CW complex as data that remembers topology: open cells, characteristic maps, attaching maps on boundaries, and a weak topology that lets local closure checks govern global continuity and closedness.

label: Open and Closed Cells
notes: An open n-cell is homeomorphic to an open n-ball, a closed n-cell to a closed ball. The radial proof shows any compact convex body with interior is a closed cell: from an interior point, each ray meets the boundary exactly once, stretching the ball to fill the body.

label: Attaching Maps
notes: Cells are assembled by maps, not by drawing. To attach an n-cell, send the boundary sphere of a closed ball into X by a continuous attaching map, then quotient. The characteristic map extends to the whole disk; its interior becomes a fresh open n-cell while the boundary lands below.

label: Skeletons and Inductive Gluing
notes: Build upward from the discrete 0-skeleton. The n-skeleton adds all n-cells attached along maps into the previous skeleton, and each skeleton is a subcomplex. Inductive proofs define data on one skeleton, extend across the next layer of cells, and use coherence to recover a global statement.

label: Conditions C and W
notes: The two letters do real work. Closure finiteness C says each closed cell meets only finitely many cells. Weak topology W says a set is closed precisely when its intersection with every closed cell is closed. Without W a sequence can pass every cell test yet still accumulate globally unaccounted.

label: The Sphere with Two Cells
notes: The simplest interesting structure: take one 0-cell as basepoint and one n-cell. The attaching map crushes the entire boundary sphere to that point. The quotient of a closed n-ball collapsing its boundary is exactly the n-sphere, giving the minimal CW decomposition with two cells total.

label: The Torus CW Structure
notes: The torus needs one 0-cell at the identified corners, two 1-cell loops a and b, and one 2-cell. The 2-cell attaches by the boundary word a b a inverse b inverse, reading the fundamental polygon edge by edge. This single relator encodes the commutator that abelianizes the fundamental group.

label: Projective Spaces
notes: Real projective space carries one cell in each dimension from zero up to n, built by attaching an n-cell to projective n-minus-one space via the antipodal quotient of the sphere. This minimal tower makes RP-n a clean computational example whose skeleton filtration matches its dimension exactly.

label: What the 1-Skeleton Knows
notes: Higher cells cannot secretly join components because their boundary already lands below. So a CW complex is connected exactly when its 1-skeleton is connected, and then it is path-connected. Compactness is finite too: compact subsets are closed and sit inside some finite subcomplex of the whole space.

label: Classifying 1-Manifolds
notes: With a regular CW structure each edge has two endpoint vertices. A boundaryless 1-manifold forces degree two at every vertex: a finite closed chain is a circle, an infinite chain is the line. Degree-one boundary vertices give a compact interval or, with one infinite direction, a half-line.

label: Simplicial Complexes
notes: A simplicial complex is a rigid subcase: closed simplices, every face included, intersections that are common faces. Its polyhedron is a regular CW complex with simplex interiors as cells. Boundary matrices satisfy d1 d2 equals zero, and Betti numbers read connectedness and holes combinatorially.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: For a finite CW complex the Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of cell counts by dimension. It is a homotopy invariant independent of the chosen decomposition. The sphere gives two, the torus gives zero, and projective plane gives one, matching every other valid cell structure.
